facts: Completed in 1846, it was the first structure in Britain built entirely of cast iron, brick and stone, with no structural wood.
It houses Tate Liverpool, the Merseyside Maritime Museum and the International Slavery Museum.
James Street is the closest Merseyrail station to Liverpool's waterfront, a UNESCO World Heritage Site until its 2021 delisting.
It is the largest cathedral in Britain and one of the largest in the world.
Architect Giles Gilbert Scott won the design competition for it aged just 22, in 1903.
Its central tower is the highest cathedral tower in the world, at 101 metres.
The museum is housed in the Albert Dock, tracing the band's history from their Liverpool roots.
All four Beatles were born and grew up in the Liverpool area.
The Cavern Club, where the band performed nearly 300 times, is a short walk from Liverpool Central station.
St George's Hall is considered one of the finest neoclassical buildings in Europe, completed in 1854.
It stands directly opposite Liverpool Lime Street station.
The hall combines a concert hall, law courts and public rooms under one roof.
The Mersey Ferry crossing has operated in some form since the 12th century, when monks rowed passengers across the river.
The song 'Ferry Cross the Mersey' by Gerry and the Pacemakers made the crossing internationally famous.
Birkenhead Hamilton Square station is one of the deepest stations in the UK, built beneath the Mersey.
Cammell Laird has built ships on the Birkenhead waterfront since 1828.
The yard built the Ark Royal aircraft carriers among many other Royal Navy vessels.
Birkenhead's shipbuilding heritage shaped much of the town's Victorian growth.
The attraction displays U-534, a German Second World War submarine raised from the seabed in 1993.
It sits at Woodside, Birkenhead's historic ferry terminal.
The submarine was cut into sections to allow it to be transported and displayed.
Southport Pier, opened in 1860, is the second-longest pleasure pier in Britain.
The town's Lord Street is said to have inspired parts of the redesign of Paris under Napoleon III, who lived there in exile.
Southport's Marine Lake was created in the 1880s as the sea receded from the original shoreline.
The Sefton Coast sand dunes are one of the largest dune systems in England.
They are home to one of the last strongholds of the red squirrel in England.
The rare natterjack toad also breeds in the dune slacks along this coast.
Formby's pinewoods are one of the best places in England to see red squirrels in the wild.
The site is managed by the National Trust, covering pine plantations and open dunes.
Formby beach also preserves ancient human and animal footprints uncovered in the mudflats.
Another Place is an installation of 100 cast-iron figures by sculptor Antony Gormley, spread along 3km of beach.
The figures, all cast from the artist's own body, face out to sea.
The installation has been on Crosby beach permanently since 2007.
Fort Perch Rock was built in the 1820s to defend the mouth of the River Mersey.
New Brighton was developed as a seaside resort from the 1830s, styled after its namesake Brighton.
The town's promenade offers wide views across Liverpool Bay.
Royal Liverpool Golf Club, at Hoylake, has hosted The Open Championship multiple times since 1897.
The club is one of the oldest links courses in England, founded in 1869.
Hoylake sits on the Wirral Peninsula, facing the Dee Estuary.
Hilbre Island can be reached on foot from West Kirby across the sands at low tide.
The island is a nature reserve known for grey seals and migrating birds.
West Kirby is the terminus of the Wirral Line branch from Liverpool.

landmark: Port Sunlight's origins (view from Bebington side)
facts: Port Sunlight, the model village built by Lever Brothers for its soap factory workers, lies across the Wirral from this line.
William Lever began building the village in 1888 to house his soap-works employees.
Hooton is a junction station on the Wirral, with connections towards Chester and Ellesmere Port.
Knowsley Safari Park opened in 1971 in the grounds of Knowsley Hall, the Earl of Derby's estate.
Prescot's Shakespeare North Playhouse, opened in 2022, is built to a design inspired by Jacobean theatres.
Prescot was historically a centre of watchmaking in England.
St Helens R.F.C. is one of English rugby league's most successful clubs.
The town's World of Glass museum reflects its history as a centre of glassmaking, home to Pilkington Glass.
St Helens Central is the main station serving the town centre.
Huyton was formerly a rural township before rapid growth as a Liverpool suburb in the 20th century.
Former Prime Minister Harold Wilson served as MP for the Huyton constituency for over 30 years.
Huyton is a key interchange point on the line towards St Helens and Wigan.
Speke Hall is one of the finest surviving Tudor timber-framed manor houses in England.
It stands close to Liverpool John Lennon Airport, a short distance from Liverpool South Parkway station.
The house is now managed by the National Trust.
Sudley House displays the art collection of shipowner George Holt in his former family home.
The house holds important works by Turner, Gainsborough and the Pre-Raphaelites.
It is one of the few Merseyside mansions to retain both its original collection and furnishings.
Sefton Park's Palm House, a Victorian glasshouse, opened in 1896.
The 235-acre park was landscaped by Edouard Andre, who also worked on Paris's parks.
It is one of Liverpool's largest and most popular green spaces.
Blackpool Pleasure Beach has operated on the same seafront site since 1896.
Its Big One rollercoaster, opened in 1994, was the tallest and fastest in the world at the time.
The station named after it sits right beside the park's entrance.
Blackpool South station serves the quieter southern end of Blackpool's famous promenade.
The town's illuminations, running each autumn, have lit the seafront since 1879.
Blackpool South is on the line that also serves Blackpool Pleasure Beach and St Annes.
Lytham's white windmill on the green has stood since 1805, rebuilt after a fire in the 1900s.
Lytham St Annes is known for its Open Championship golf links course, Royal Lytham & St Annes.
Lytham's seafront green is one of the largest of its kind on the Lancashire coast.
St Annes Pier opened in 1885 as part of the resort's Victorian development.
St Annes was purpose-built as a genteel seaside resort, in contrast to nearby Blackpool.
The town later merged with Lytham to form Lytham St Annes.
Ormskirk's parish church is unusual in having both a tower and a separate spire, a rare combination in England.
The town holds one of Lancashire's oldest street markets, dating back to a 13th-century charter.
Ormskirk is the northern terminus of one branch of the Merseyrail Northern Line.
Aintree Racecourse hosts the Grand National, the world's most famous steeplechase, established in 1839.
Croxteth Hall, a former stately home, sits within a country park a short distance from the racecourse.
Aintree station serves the racecourse directly on race days.
Wallasey's promenade stretches along the Irish Sea coast of the Wirral.
The town's Kings Parade was a fashionable Victorian and Edwardian seafront development.
Wallasey Village station is one of two Merseyrail stations serving the town, alongside Wallasey Grove Road.
Eastham Country Park overlooks the entrance to the Manchester Ship Canal on the Mersey.
The park was a popular Victorian pleasure garden, reached by paddle steamer from Liverpool.
Hooton station is a key Wirral junction on the way towards Ellesmere Port.
Rufford Old Hall is a 15th-century timber-framed manor house, one of the finest in Lancashire.
Its Great Hall retains an original medieval hammerbeam roof.
The hall is now owned by the National Trust.
Burscough sits at the junction of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal and the Rufford Branch Canal.
Burscough Junction station is where the Ormskirk and Southport branches of the Merseyrail network meet.
The village grew as a canal and agricultural trading centre in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Astley Hall, near Chorley, is a grand Elizabethan and Jacobean house set in parkland.
Euxton Balshaw Lane station sits at a key junction on the West Coast Main Line approaches to Preston.
The surrounding area of Chorley grew as a cotton-milling town in the Industrial Revolution.

landmark: Heysham Port & the Isle of Man ferry
facts: Heysham Port operates regular ferry services to the Isle of Man and Northern Ireland.
The station sits right beside the ferry terminal, a rare direct rail-to-ferry link.
Heysham also has two nuclear power stations nearby, though the port itself is Lancashire's main sea link to the Isle of Man.
Millom grew rapidly in the 19th century around its ironworks, now long closed.
The town sits at the mouth of the Duddon Estuary on the edge of the Lake District.
Millom's Folk Museum reflects its industrial ironworking past.
Askam grew from a hamlet into a planned industrial town after ironstone was discovered nearby in the 1850s.
The village overlooks the sands of the Duddon Estuary.
Askam sits on the scenic Cumbrian Coast Line.

landmark: Conway Park's underground Wirral Line hub
facts: Conway Park station, opened in 1998, is one of the newest stations on the Wirral Line.
It was built as part of a regeneration scheme in central Birkenhead.
The station sits largely underground, close to Birkenhead town centre.
Bidston Hill offers panoramic views across the Mersey to Liverpool's waterfront.
A restored 200-year-old windmill stands on Bidston Hill.
Bidston is a key Wirral junction where the West Kirby and New Brighton branches split.
Eccleston Park lies within the Metropolitan Borough of St Helens, close to the Knowsley border.
The area developed largely as a residential suburb serving St Helens' glass and industrial works.
The station is a request stop on the line between Liverpool and Wigan.
Garswood sits within what was once the Lancashire coalfield, a major mining area until the mid-20th century.
The village grew around collieries that have since closed.
Garswood station is on the line between Liverpool and Wigan.
Hunts Cross is the southern terminus of the Merseyrail Northern Line electrified service.
It is also an interchange with Northern's services towards Warrington and Manchester.
The area developed as a Liverpool suburb in the early 20th century.

landmark: Halewood & the Jaguar Land Rover plant
facts: Halewood is home to a major Jaguar Land Rover car manufacturing plant, opened in 1963.
The plant has built vehicles for Ford, Jaguar and Land Rover at different points in its history.
Halewood station sits on the Liverpool to Warrington/Manchester line.
Bootle was once home to some of the busiest docks on the River Mersey.
The town suffered heavy bombing during the Liverpool Blitz of 1940-41 due to its dockland importance.
Bootle New Strand serves the town's main shopping centre, built as part of post-war redevelopment.
Waterloo, Merseyside, takes its name from a house built to commemorate the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.
The town's promenade links towards Crosby beach and the Antony Gormley 'Another Place' statues.
Waterloo station is a key interchange on the Merseyrail Northern Line towards Southport.
Aughton Park station serves a quiet residential area between Ormskirk and Town Green.
The wider Aughton area retains a rural, semi-agricultural character despite its proximity to Liverpool.
It is one of the smaller stops on the Ormskirk branch of the Northern Line.
Freshfield station is a popular access point for the National Trust's Formby red squirrel reserve.
The surrounding pinewoods were planted in the 19th century to help stabilise the coastal dunes.
Freshfield sits between Formby and Ainsdale on the Sefton coast line.
Birkdale developed as an exclusive Victorian seaside suburb of Southport.
Royal Birkdale Golf Club, nearby, has hosted The Open Championship multiple times.
Birkdale station retains much of its original Victorian character.
Kirkby was designated a major post-war overspill town for Liverpool from the late 1940s.
It became home to one of the largest council housing estates in Europe at the time.
Kirkby is the eastern terminus of one branch of the Merseyrail Northern Line.
Headbolt Lane opened in 2023 as the newest station on the Merseyrail network, extending the line beyond Kirkby.
It was built with hydrogen train trials in mind, alongside conventional electric services.
The station serves a residential area on the northern edge of Kirkby.
Edge Hill is recognised as the oldest passenger railway station still in use in the world.
It opened in 1836 as part of the pioneering Liverpool and Manchester Railway.
The station retains sections of its original 19th-century platforms and cutting.
Stanlow is one of the largest oil refineries in the United Kingdom.
It has operated on the Mersey estuary since the 1920s.
Stanlow & Thornton station sits on the Wirral Line between Ellesmere Port and Helsby.

landmark: Port Sunlight Village & Lady Lever Art Gallery
facts: Port Sunlight was built by William Lever from 1888 to house workers at his Sunlight Soap factory.
The village is now a Grade II listed conservation area with over 900 listed buildings.
The Lady Lever Art Gallery, founded by Lever in memory of his wife, holds one of the finest Pre-Raphaelite collections in Britain.
The museum sits at the historic junction of the Shropshire Union Canal and the Manchester Ship Canal.
It holds one of the largest collections of historic canal boats in Britain.
Ellesmere Port grew rapidly in the 19th century as a canal and later dock town.

landmark: Liverpool ONE & the city centre loop
facts: Moorfields is one of four underground stations forming Liverpool's central Merseyrail loop, opened in 1977.
It sits close to Liverpool ONE, a major open-air shopping and leisure quarter opened in 2008.
The Liverpool loop line runs beneath the city centre, connecting the Northern and Wirral lines.
Sellafield has been a centre of Britain's nuclear industry since the 1950s, including the world's first commercial nuclear power station.
It is now primarily a nuclear decommissioning and waste management site.
Sellafield station serves the large workforce commuting to the site daily.
Nicknamed 'La'al Ratty', it is one of the oldest and longest-running narrow-gauge heritage railways in England.
It originally opened in 1875 to carry iron ore from mines in Eskdale.
The heritage railway connects directly with the main line at Ravenglass station.
Muncaster Castle has been owned by the Pennington family for over 800 years.
Its grounds include the World Owl Centre, home to one of the largest owl collections in Britain.
The castle overlooks the Esk Valley on the edge of the Lake District.

landmark: Walls Castle Roman Bath House, Ravenglass
facts: Walls Castle is the best-preserved Roman building in northern England, with walls still standing over 4 metres high.
It was part of a Roman fort called Glannaventa, guarding the Cumbrian coast.
Ravenglass is the only coastal town within the Lake District National Park.
St Bees Priory was founded around 1120, on a site linked to the 7th-century Irish saint Bega.
The priory church still serves as the parish church of St Bees today.
St Bees is a well-preserved sandstone village on the Cumbrian coast.
St Bees Head is the official starting point of Alfred Wainwright's Coast to Coast walk.
The sandstone cliffs are the only significant cliff coastline in Cumbria, home to nesting seabirds.
It also marks the westernmost point of northern England.
The Beacon tells the story of Whitehaven's harbour, once one of Britain's busiest ports for the rum and tobacco trade.
Whitehaven was laid out on a grid plan in the 17th century, an early example of British town planning.
The Washington family, ancestors of George Washington, had strong historical links to Whitehaven.
Whitehaven's harbour was attacked by American naval officer John Paul Jones in 1778, one of the last hostile landings on English soil.
The harbour once handled more coal exports than any other English port outside London.
Whitehaven's Georgian streets are considered among the best-preserved in England.
Whitehaven has a strong rugby league tradition alongside its maritime history.
The town's coal-mining past shaped much of its surrounding landscape and communities.
Whitehaven sits on the Cumbrian Coast Line between Barrow and Carlisle.
Silecroft has one of the longest sandy beaches on the Cumbrian coast, backed by dunes.
The village sits beneath Black Combe, a distinctive standalone fell.
Silecroft station is a small request stop on the line.
Black Combe rises to 600 metres and is said to offer views across parts of five countries on a clear day.
The fell was described by William Wordsworth in his poem 'View from the Top of Black Comb'.
It stands somewhat isolated from the main Lake District fells, close to the coast.
Kirkby-in-Furness sits on the Duddon Estuary, on the southwestern fringe of the Lake District.
The village was historically linked to slate quarrying in the surrounding fells.
It offers views across the estuary towards Millom and the sea.
Green Road is one of the smallest and least-used stations on the Cumbrian Coast Line.
It overlooks the tidal sands of the Duddon Estuary.
The station serves a scattered rural community rather than a single village centre.
Bootle, Cumbria, is a small village distinct from the larger Bootle in Merseyside.
It sits between the fells and the sea on the quiet Cumbrian Coast Line.
The village church dates back to medieval times, though much altered since.
Eskmeals Dunes are an important site for rare coastal plants and natterjack toads.
The dunes sit near the mouth of the River Esk on the Cumbrian coast.
The area also has a long history as a military weapons testing range.
Braystones is known for a small cluster of distinctive beach chalets built directly on the shore.
The station is a minor request stop on the Cumbrian Coast Line.
It sits between Sellafield and St Bees on the coast.
Nethertown is one of the least-used stations in England, serving a small rural hamlet.
It sits on the Cumbrian coast between St Bees and Sellafield.
The beach here is a quiet, little-visited stretch of shoreline.
Corkickle sits at the southern edge of Whitehaven, close to the town's Georgian conservation area.
It was once linked to Whitehaven's extensive coal mining tunnels, which extended out under the sea.
Corkickle station is a short walk from Whitehaven's harbour area.
Drigg is home to the UK's principal disposal facility for low-level radioactive waste.
The village also sits close to Drigg Dunes, a nature reserve important for natterjack toads.
Drigg station serves both the village and the nearby Sellafield workforce.
Seascale developed as a small Victorian seaside resort, with a golf course along the shore.
The village sits close to Sellafield, a short distance up the coast.
Seascale's beach looks out across the Irish Sea towards the Isle of Man on clear days.

landmark: Coast to Coast Walk start point
facts: Walkers traditionally dip a boot in the Irish Sea at St Bees before setting off across England to Robin Hood's Bay.
The 192-mile route was devised by fellwalker Alfred Wainwright in 1973.
St Bees marks the western end of this coast-to-coast crossing of northern England.
The Rum Story museum, in a former wine and spirit merchant's cellars, traces Whitehaven's role in the rum trade.
Whitehaven imported sugar and rum from the Caribbean, closely tied to the transatlantic slave trade.
The town's harbour still has three historic piers from its 18th-century trading heyday.
Sellafield remains one of the largest employers in West Cumbria.
The surrounding coastline includes stretches managed for nature conservation despite the industrial site.
The site has operated under several names, including Windscale, since it opened in the 1940s and 50s.
Muncaster Castle is often described as one of the most haunted houses in England.
Its Tapestry Room is said to be haunted by the ghost of a murdered court jester, Tom Fool.
The castle's gardens include a maze and extensive rhododendron collection.
Whitehaven's Haig Pit mined coal from tunnels that extended more than five miles out under the Irish Sea.
The pit closed in 1986, ending centuries of coal mining in the town.
The former colliery site is now home to a mining and energy heritage centre.
Silecroft is a popular starting point for walks up Black Combe.
The beach here is one of the quietest and least developed on the Cumbrian coast.
The village sits within the Lake District National Park boundary.
Ravenglass sits where three rivers, the Esk, Mite and Irt, meet the sea.
It is the only coastal settlement inside the Lake District National Park.
The estuary is an important habitat for wading birds and waterfowl.
St Bees is built largely from local red sandstone, giving the village a distinctive warm colour.
St Bees School, founded in 1583, is one of the oldest schools in Cumbria.
The village sits just south of the sandstone cliffs of St Bees Head.
The fells above Kirkby-in-Furness were once extensively quarried for green slate.
Burlington slate from this area has been used in prestigious buildings worldwide.
The village looks out across the sands of the Duddon Estuary at low tide.
Seascale Golf Club, founded in 1893, is one of the oldest links courses on the Cumbrian coast.
The course runs along the dunes between the village and the sea.
Seascale developed largely as a planned Victorian resort, with wide tree-lined streets.
Whitehaven's candlestick chimney and harbour lighthouses are iconic features of its historic waterfront.
The town was one of the first in England to be built on a formal grid-street plan, from the 1680s.
Whitehaven's population briefly rivalled that of Liverpool in the 18th century, at the height of its trade.
The Roman fort at Ravenglass, Glannaventa, once housed a garrison guarding the Cumbrian coast.
Its bath house walls survive to an unusual height for a Roman ruin in Britain.
Ravenglass was a strategic harbour for Roman supply ships along the coast.
The waters off St Bees Head have a long history of shipwrecks due to the rocky coastline.
St Bees Head has two lighthouses guiding vessels along this stretch of coast.
The cliffs are a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest for breeding seabirds.
The England Coast Path passes close to Sellafield, linking the surrounding villages.
Sellafield sits between the Lake District fells and the Irish Sea.
The site has been a major driver of employment in West Cumbria for over 70 years.
Millom, a short distance from Kirkby-in-Furness, grew rapidly around iron ore mining in the 19th century.
The poet Norman Nicholson, born in Millom, wrote extensively about the town and its industry.
The Duddon Estuary separates Kirkby-in-Furness from Millom across the sands.
St Nicholas' tower is one of the few remaining parts of Whitehaven's original 17th-century parish church.
The rest of the church was largely destroyed by fire in the 1970s.
It stands at the heart of Whitehaven's planned Georgian street grid.
Eskdale, reached from Ravenglass, is one of the quieter valleys of the Lake District.
Scafell Pike, England's highest mountain, lies at the head of the valley.
The narrow-gauge railway climbs gradually into the valley from the coast.

landmark: Seascale's sea views to the Isle of Man
facts: On exceptionally clear days, the Isle of Man is visible from Seascale's beach.
The village was once considered as a potential larger seaside resort in the Victorian era.
Seascale sits almost midway along the Cumbrian Coast Line.
Drigg Dunes is one of the largest sand dune systems in northwest England.
It supports rare natterjack toads and a wide range of coastal plant species.
The reserve is managed by Cumbria Wildlife Trust.
St Bees has one of the few sand and shingle beaches on this stretch of the Cumbrian coast.
It looks out towards the Isle of Man and, on clear days, the Scottish coast.
The beach sits directly below the sandstone cliffs of St Bees Head.
The small chalets at Braystones sit unusually close to the high-tide line, built up over decades.
The settlement has no shop or pub, remaining a very quiet coastal spot.
Braystones is one of the request stops on the Cumbrian Coast Line, trains stopping only if flagged down or requested.
Whitehaven has hosted large maritime festivals celebrating its harbour and sailing heritage.
The harbour's historic sea walls and piers remain largely as built in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Whitehaven was one of the first planned towns in England, laid out from 1660 onward.
The coastal path at Nethertown links St Bees Head to the wider Cumbrian Coast Path.
Nethertown is one of the quietest halts on the entire line, with only a handful of daily trains.
The settlement consists of little more than a scattering of houses near the shore.
Corkickle is one of the smallest stations on the Cumbrian Coast Line, a simple halt with minimal facilities.
It sits within walking distance of Whitehaven town centre.
The area was historically linked to Whitehaven's extensive underground coal workings.
Green Road station overlooks the wide tidal sands of the Duddon Estuary.
It serves one of the smallest catchment populations on the line.
The Duddon Estuary is an important area for wading birds at low tide.
Bootle's parish church has origins going back centuries, though much rebuilt over time.
The village sits inland slightly from the coast, in quiet farmland.
Bootle, Cumbria, should not be confused with the larger town of the same name near Liverpool.

landmark: Silecroft's views to the Isle of Man
facts: Silecroft's beach offers clear views out across the Irish Sea on good days.
The village is a quiet base for walkers heading up onto Black Combe.
Silecroft sits on the western fringe of the Lake District National Park boundary.
Muncaster Fell offers a ridge walk with views across the Eskdale valley to the high fells beyond.
The route can be combined with a ride on the Ravenglass and Eskdale Railway.
It is a popular, relatively gentle fell walk compared to the higher Lakeland peaks.

landmark: Kirkby-in-Furness viewpoint over the Duddon Sands
facts: The village offers sweeping views across the Duddon Sands towards Millom and the sea.
Kirkby-in-Furness is a starting point for walks up onto the surrounding slate fells.
The area was once dotted with small quarries supplying green slate for roofing.
Seascale's wide, tree-lined streets reflect its planned development as a Victorian seaside resort.
The village was intended to rival larger resorts further afield but remained relatively small.
Seascale station still serves both residents and Sellafield commuters today.
